0113.04a1Organizational.2.statementText: The organization shall establish, document, and disseminate an information security policy.

0226.09k1Organizational.2.statementText: Contractual clause referencing AT&T Test requirements.

UNKNOWN-ID-999.statementText: This control id does not exist in the registered v11.8.0 e1 set.

e1-01-01.topicSummary: e1 requires a leadership-endorsed information security policy that has actually been communicated to the workforce, not merely drafted. It must state its own scope and objectives, demonstrate visible management commitment to security, assign clear ownership of security responsibilities across management and staff, and describe the organization's overall approach to protecting information.

e1-02-01.topicSummary: e1 requires current anti-malware/anti-spyware (or comparable malicious-code detection) software installed and kept up to date across all in-scope endpoints -- workstations, laptops, and servers -- as a baseline defense against common malicious code.

e1-02-02.topicSummary: Those same endpoints also need a host-based firewall or equivalent port-filtering control configured to deny all inbound/outbound traffic by default, permitting only specific ports or services that have been explicitly authorized as exceptions.

e1-03-01.topicSummary: This domain governs how removable and portable storage media may be used with organizational systems -- restricting writable removable media and barring personally-owned removable devices -- and, per the v11.8 baseline refresh, requires digital portable media leaving controlled areas to be cryptographically protected in transit, while both digital and non-digital portable media must carry documented accountability and be handled only by authorized personnel.

e1-04-01.topicLabel: Full-Disk Encryption of Mobile Endpoints Handling Sensitive Data
e1-04-01.topicSummary: The Mobile Device Security domain's e1 scope reduces to a single expectation: any mobile computing endpoint -- laptops included, not just phones and tablets -- that stores, processes, or transmits sensitive data must have full-disk encryption enabled, with avoiding sensitive data on such devices altogether framed as an even stronger posture. Broader MDM/BYOD practices (enrollment, remote wipe, app containerization) sit outside the e1 baseline and only appear at higher assurance tiers.

e1-05-01.topicSummary: e1's Wireless Security scope is narrow: wireless network access must be explicitly and formally approved before use, and any wireless access points or devices connecting to the network must use strong encryption (at minimum an AES-based WPA2 standard) to protect both authentication and data in transit. Avoiding wireless transmission of sensitive data altogether is noted as a preferable alternative where feasible.

e1-06-01.topicSummary: Changes to infrastructure, applications, and user access should follow a formal request-assess-test-approve cycle rather than being made ad hoc, with approval coming from someone other than the requester. Lightweight tracking such as a spreadsheet is sufficient at this level -- a dedicated change-management platform is not required.

e1-06-02.topicSummary: Systems should be deployed against a documented hardening baseline or configuration checklist rather than left at vendor defaults, with resources such as the CIS Benchmarks cited as a practical way to define that baseline -- reducing attack surface through configuration standards independent of patch level.

e1-07-01.topicSummary: In-scope systems must be kept on supported, currently-patched software versions. Automated tooling is preferred for applying and enforcing these updates, with a documented, manually-tracked patching process expected as the fallback wherever automated patching isn't operationally feasible.

e1-07-02.topicSummary: Organizations are expected to maintain a current inventory of technology assets and data repositories (e.g., databases), including personally-owned/BYOD devices connecting to the network or cloud environment, reviewed on a recurring (at least annual) basis so vulnerability management has full visibility into what needs assessment.
e1-07-02.reviewNote: A fresh v11.8 compile pass (2026-07-21) proposed this same topic and its adversarial verifier rejected it for resting solely on this one individual's non-authoritative LinkedIn Pulse post, additionally noting the page may be login-gated and unreliable to fetch. The identical single-source weakness applies to this carried-forward entry -- no independent corroborating citation has been found -- so it is flagged here as the domain's weakest-sourced item rather than dropped.

e1-07-03.topicSummary: e1 expects recurring vulnerability scanning, at minimum yearly, across any asset that stores, processes, or transmits sensitive information -- extending beyond traditional network/host scanning to cover cloud configuration review, application-level testing, and monitoring of third-party software dependencies where applicable.

e1-08-01.topicSummary: Internal and external networks must be logically separated using an isolated buffer zone (DMZ-style screened subnet) rather than exposing internal systems directly to outside traffic, enforced through standard perimeter devices -- firewalls, ACL-enabled routers, cloud security groups, and web application firewalls. Wireless networks must sit behind their own firewall boundary, and sensitive data should live on segments purpose-built for it, apart from lower-trust traffic.

e1-08-02.topicSummary: Outbound DNS lookups should be filtered against known-malicious domain reputation data (DNS sinkholing or an equivalent service) so devices attempting to reach malicious or command-and-control domains are redirected or blocked. Both free (e.g., a U.S. government-provided option) and commercial DNS filtering services are cited as acceptable ways to satisfy this.

e1-09-01.topicSummary: Sender-authentication protocols (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) should be configured for the organization's email-sending domain(s) so messages spoofing or impersonating the domain can be detected and rejected, targeting phishing and business-email-compromise that relies on domain impersonation.

e1-09-02.topicSummary: Basic email filtering should be implemented at the server level to block suspicious inbound messages and risky or unnecessary attachment file types -- typically satisfied out-of-the-box by standard hosted email platforms (e.g., Microsoft 365, Google Workspace) without extra tooling.

e1-10-01.topicSummary: HITRUST's own published sample e1 validated assessment report shows this domain populated by the legacy control area "User Password Management," listed as an in-scope, implementable control for e1. At the topic level this covers an organization's baseline practices for issuing, tracking, and managing user account credentials as foundational access-control hygiene, rather than a fully detailed technical password standard -- no verbatim requirement wording is publicly available for this domain.

e1-10-02.topicLabel: Enforced Password Policy via Technical Controls
e1-10-02.topicSummary: A defined password policy calling for strong passwords should be enforced through technical means (system-enforced settings) rather than relying on documentation alone; independent commentary notes HITRUST does not itself specify a precise entropy/strength threshold, leaving that judgment to the assessor.

e1-11-01.topicSummary: Requests for system access should go through a formal request-and-approval step before being securely provisioned, and every account should map to a single identifiable person rather than being shared. When someone's role changes or employment ends, their access should be modified or removed promptly.

e1-11-02.topicSummary: Accounts should lock automatically after a set number of failed sign-in attempts to blunt password-guessing attacks, and end-user devices should be configured to lock the screen after a period of inactivity so an unattended, already-authenticated session can't be misused.
e1-11-02.reviewNote: A fresh v11.8 compile pass (2026-07-21) proposed this same topic and its adversarial verifier rejected it for resting solely on this one individual's non-authoritative LinkedIn Pulse post, raising doubt about whether the page's content was genuinely fetched versus confabulated against a login wall. The identical single-source weakness applies to this carried-forward entry -- no independent corroborating citation has been found -- so it is flagged here as one of the domain's weaker-sourced items rather than dropped.

e1-11-03.topicSummary: Access to systems and services should be limited to what a person's role actually requires, using role-based permissions rather than broad default access. Administrative or privileged tasks should be performed from an account distinct from an individual's everyday user account, a distinction emphasized especially in directory-services environments such as Active Directory.

e1-11-04.topicSummary: Anyone connecting to the network remotely, or using an administrative/privileged account even from a local device, is expected to authenticate with more than a single factor, directly addressing credential-theft and brute-force attack scenarios that e1 targets.

e1-11-05.topicLabel: Periodic Review of User Access Rights
e1-11-05.topicSummary: On at least a yearly cadence, the organization is expected to formally re-examine user accounts, their privileges, and group memberships to confirm continued business need, keeping a record of what was reviewed and any resulting corrective action.

e1-12-01.topicLabel: Complete, Tamper-Protected Audit Trail for Sensitive-Data Access
e1-12-01.topicSummary: This domain expects organizations to keep thorough records of who accessed or changed systems, applications, and assets holding sensitive information, and to ensure those records can't be quietly altered, deleted, or otherwise tampered with by unauthorized parties, giving the organization a reliable trail for detecting and investigating suspicious activity.

e1-13-01.topicLabel: Controlling Unauthorized Software Installation and Training Staff to Evaluate Software
e1-13-01.topicSummary: This pairs a technical safeguard with a people-side one: endpoints should be locked down so employees can't install applications outside what's sanctioned, while relevant staff are also given grounding in how to vet a piece of software before it's adopted for use -- a hard technical control alongside a lighter-touch training element.
e1-13-01.reviewNote: This entry rests solely on the same non-authoritative LinkedIn Pulse post as e1-07-02 and e1-11-02, with no independent corroborating citation. It was not re-proposed by the 2026-07-21 refresh compile run, so there is no fresh rejection (or re-shipment) evidence for it specifically, but the identical single-source weakness applies and it is flagged here for consistency rather than only scrutinizing entries the refresh run happened to re-test.

e1-13-02.topicLabel: Onboarding and Annual Security Awareness Training (Phishing Recognition & Reporting)
e1-13-02.topicSummary: Every workforce member is expected to complete a baseline security-awareness course upon joining, plus some form of refresher for all staff at least once a year. The skill being built is recognizing social-engineering attempts -- phishing as the headline example -- and knowing how to flag a suspicious message rather than act on it.

e1-14-01.topicLabel: Restricting and Time-Limiting Third-Party Remote Access
e1-14-01.topicSummary: The Third-Party Assurance domain's e1 scope narrows to one focus area: any remote or external access granted to third parties/vendors must be limited strictly to what their role requires, bounded in duration (e.g., session or connection timeouts), and promptly revoked once no longer needed -- distinct from the broader vendor-management topics (contracting, due diligence, ongoing monitoring) found in fuller HITRUST assessments.

e1-15-01.topicSummary: HITRUST e1's Incident Management scope is narrow, centering on the organization having a documented process for handling security incidents, making sure staff are made aware of it, and periodically checking that the process still matches how incidents are actually handled in practice.
e1-15-01.reviewNote: Reinstated during maintainer review after verification rejected the original candidate over an unsupported 'held through CSF v11.8' persistence claim; that clause and its unsupporting second citation were removed, leaving only the core claim the verifier explicitly confirmed as citation-supported.

e1-16-01.topicSummary: Backup copies of critical data are expected to be kept at a location geographically separate/remote from the source systems, and the backup process along with the actual ability to restore data is expected to be periodically verified through testing (secondary sources describe roughly a monthly cadence) rather than assumed to work.

e1-16-02.topicSummary: Organizations are expected to maintain backups of data that are either kept offline (physically or logically disconnected from production networks) or made immutable (protected against modification or deletion, e.g., via retention-locked storage), so that a ransomware attack or a compromised administrator account cannot also destroy or alter the backup copies.
e1-16-02.reviewNote: The 'this requirement has reportedly remained part of the e1 baseline through CSF v11.8' claim and its unverified controlReference were removed during maintainer review -- neither citation specifically confirms persistence through v11.8, the same unsupported-overclaim pattern that caused a similarly-worded Incident Management candidate to be rejected in verification.

e1-17-01.topicSummary: HITRUST's Risk Management domain at e1 is represented by a single, narrow topic: running a basic risk-assessment practice on a regular cadence -- at minimum annually, and again whenever the environment changes materially (new systems, new threats, major organizational change). Broader risk-treatment/mitigation-planning content (deciding how to respond to identified risks) sits outside the e1 baseline and appears only at higher assurance tiers.

e1-18-01.topicLabel: Documented Destruction of Retired Media and Equipment
e1-18-01.topicSummary: When storage media, drives, or equipment that once held sensitive information reach end of life, the organization is expected to physically destroy them and keep records evidencing that the destruction actually took place.

e1-18-02.topicLabel: Restricted Physical Access to Sensitive Data Areas
e1-18-02.topicSummary: Physical access to locations that store, process, or transmit sensitive information (such as data centers and server rooms) should be limited to individuals who have been specifically and formally authorized, rather than left generally accessible to staff.

e1-19-01.topicLabel: Public Posting / Social Media Information Controls
e1-19-01.topicSummary: This domain's e1 contribution is a single baseline item: restricting who may publish content to public-facing or publicly accessible systems (including social media), so only authorized personnel post material and only information cleared for public release goes out -- narrower than the broader data-classification/retention/disposal/privacy-incident-response scope this domain covers at higher assessment tiers.
